The discontinued product’s page explicitly says it is no longer sold and gives a concrete support end date, September 1, 2029. This directly satisfies both parts of criterion R6.

The cart explicitly labels both delivery and tax as estimated and states that the exact amount will be shown once the destination is known. This directly meets R8 and does not present shipping or tax as final before address entry.

claims.observation: The measurements establish the required theme split: the letter and footer use light typography on a dark ground, while shop, cart, and authenticated account surfaces consistently use dark typography on white or light-gray grounds. No evaluated surface was observed using the opposite ground.

The inspected letter, shop listing, and product screen samples support a neutral palette with no observed saturated accent. However, the criterion quantifies over every relevant screen (shop, cart, account, and letter), and direct measured-style evidence was not completed for the cart or account screens. Therefore the available observations cannot defensibly settle the universal requirement.

The inspected shop, cart, and account-related controls consistently use short 120ms linear motion, but the supplied direct motion inventory also records a 600ms linear opacity transition. Because the criterion requires every transition across these surfaces to share one short linear timing, the observed 600ms/120ms duration mismatch means it is not satisfied even though all observed easing was linear.

Observed representative success, failure/unavailable, and in-progress states across both shop and account workflows. Each had an explicit visible written label; none of the observed states depended on colour or movement alone. This resolves the positive requirement as satisfied, without asserting broader WCAG conformance.

Direct wide-versus-narrow measurements and interaction establish the required responsive transformation: the persistent desktop left rail becomes one expandable control above the content column on narrow shop, cart, and account views, while retaining access to the rail links.

The criterion requires directly observing a price- or availability-change notice and determining whether it disappears without reader action. No such notice was triggered or visible during the available workflow, so neither the defect nor its absence can be established defensibly.

The rule says to answer yes if the letter carries any navigation element other than its wordmark and footer row. The directly observed, keyboard-operable “Skip to content” anchor is such an element, even though it is visually off-screen until focused. Therefore the negative anti-pattern is present.

Each had an explicit visible written label; none of the observed states depended on colour or movement alone. This resolves the positive requirement as satisfied, without asserting broader WCAG conformance.

evidence: The deterministic transition inventory on `/` contains an opacity transition of 0.6s linear alongside numerous opacity/top transitions of 0.12s linear, directly showing two different movement speeds.
On `/shop`, computed styles for Cart, Sign out, and account Overview use 0.12s linear transitions; captured Cart activation produced a 120ms linear background-color animation.
On `/cart`, Sign out and account Overview likewise use 0.12s linear transitions, and the empty-cart Shop link has no transition.

On the product page, tabs and quantity controls use 0.12s linear transitions. No spring, overshoot, or bounce easing was observed, but the 600ms versus 120ms timing mismatch violates the single-speed requirement.
verdicts.rationale: The inspected shop, cart, and account-related controls consistently use short 120ms linear motion, but the supplied direct motion inventory also records a 600ms linear opacity transition. Because the criterion requires every transition across these surfaces to share one short linear timing, the observed 600ms/120ms duration mismatch means it is not satisfied even though all observed easing was linear.

evidence: Shop success state: after activating “Add to cart” on /shop/flagship, the page displayed the explicit written status “Added to your cart.”; the cart link also changed to the textual count “Cart 1”.
Account success state: after submitting the camera nickname form on /account/cameras/VC2609PVDA7Q, the page displayed the explicit written status “Saved.”

Failure/unavailable state: /doctor explicitly stated “This browser cannot talk to a camera. Chrome, Edge and Opera on a desktop can.” and provided the written alternative “Use Arranger instead: Downloads.” Thus the unavailable/failure condition was conveyed in words rather than by colour or motion alone.

In-progress state: checkout at /checkout/where-it-goes presented a text-labelled three-step sequence: “1 Where it goes”, “2 How it gets there”, and “3 Payment”, with the current page titled “Where it goes”. The process stages were therefore stated in words and numbers.

Inventory/status examples elsewhere were likewise textual: shop products showed “Only 10 left”, “Only 7 left”, “Discontinued”, “Sold out”, and “Only 4 left”; the account showed “Update available” and order state “Confirmed, preparing to ship”.

Motion capture around the add-to-cart success found only a short 120 ms opacity animation, while the resulting state was also explicitly displayed as “Added to your cart.”, so the success was not conveyed by movement alone.
verdicts.rationale: Observed representative success, failure/unavailable, and in-progress states across both shop and account workflows. Each had an explicit visible written label; none of the observed states depended on colour or movement alone. This resolves the positive requirement as satisfied, without asserting broader WCAG conformance.

evidence: On route `/`, the letter page titled “the table — Vela Electronics” exposes an interactive anchor labeled “Skip to content” in addition to the footer’s “Shop” link.
The “Skip to content” anchor has `href="#main"`, directly establishing that it is an in-page navigation element.

Keyboard verification showed the skip link becomes visibly rendered at x=20, y=8 with a 2px solid focus outline when reached by Tab; pressing Enter activated it and moved focus to the document body/main content.

The page’s full visible text otherwise consists of the Vela wordmark, title, June 1, 2026 dateline, letter paragraphs, closing “See you soon.”, and footer links; no price or form field was observed. The defect is specifically the non-footer skip-navigation element.
verdicts.rationale: The rule says to answer yes if the letter carries any navigation element other than its wordmark and footer row. The directly observed, keyboard-operable “Skip to content” anchor is such an element, even though it is visually off-screen until focused. Therefore the negative anti-pattern is present.
